newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts shaken after Astra H 1.
newsitem.headline: Analysts shaken after Astra H 1.

text.p: Swedish drugs company Astra AB posted disappointing earnings for the first half of 1997 on Friday, but sought to reassure investors by saying growth should pick up again next year.
Analysts, however, said they were concerned about the hole left as the group's key anti-ulcer drug Losec matures and the share fell five percent on the Stockholm bourse after the results news.

Astra posted a 13-percent rise in sales to 21.47 billion crowns, in line with expectations, but the group's four percent increase in pre-tax profits to 7.01 billion crowns was lower than market forecasts of 7.18 billion.
"Growth is levelling off somewhat but will pick up later," Astra's chief executive Hakan Mogren told a news conference.
"We are on our way to getting approval for a number of significant products," he added.
The group said it expected to increase market share for its main seller Losec to 45 percent from its current 35 percent in the United States, where it is marketed under the brand name Prilosec.

Astra also said research and development (R&D) costs, which rose 22 percent to 3.99 billion crowns in the period, would increase faster than sales in 1997 but its increased marketing efforts would give short-term and long-term benefits.
But analysts, particularly disappointed by an operating profit of 6.75 billion crowns for the period versus 6.30 billion crowns a year ago, said Astra faced an uphill battle.
"The Astra story is starting to look more and more suspect," said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Steve Putnam.
"The numbers were a bit disappointing...especially as people were expecting to see a rebound from a weak first quarter that was affected by stockpiling in late 1996," Putnam said.
Astra said its North America sales rose to 6.33 billion crowns from 4.81 billion crowns which, calculated at constant rates, was a rise of 18 percent.

Sales rose nine percent in Germany, eight percent in Italy and 12 percent in The Netherlands but slipped 14 percent in Britain mainly as a result of parallel trade and fell 22 percent in Sweden, largely due to stockpiling and to parallel imports.
Under EU legislation, pharmacists can seek cheaper prices for the same drugs by buying through what are known as parallel importers.

"They face an enormous challenge given the size of Losec and I think they will continue to struggle and underperform the sector in terms of sales and earnings progressively," said analyst Jan Dworsky from CI Nordic Securities.
"We are negative on the stock and will continue to be so for sometime," Dworsky told Reuters.
Sales of Losec, its largest product which will see its patent expire in 2001, rose to 14.72 billion crowns worldwide from 11.78 billion crowns a year ago.
Astra's own sales of Losec, which it markets jointly in the U.S. with Merck Inc, rose to 10.12 billion crowns from 8.55 billion crowns.
Putnam said it did not look like Astra's R&D had yet produced anything to bale the company out.

"They may have to start to look at corporate measures, with talk about whether they are a possible takeover target for the cash flow or whether they could try to take over the complete Astra/Merck joint venture," Putnam said.
Sales of the anti-asthma agent Pulmicort rose eight percent to 2.48 billion crowns.

"I would be quite relaxed about this report if the growth rate was going to accelerate but I am not convinced that what they are doing will accelerate growth," said Morgan Stanley analyst James McKean.
"They are doing all the right things strategically but there is a lot of uncertainty out there," said McKean.
Astra closed down 10.5 crowns to 142 crowns.
